title: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia
hookLine: a leader honored as the king of the community

cards: A boy is singing in a household in Delhi.
His father has died, and his mother has brought him a long way from Punjab, to the home of Mata Sundari, Guru Gobind Singh's widow, the woman whose letters guided the scattered sangats.
Tradition says she took the boy in, and the household got used to hearing him sing the morning hymns.
Years later, that boy would ride at the head of the Dal Khalsa, and Sikhs would give him a title that sounds like a crown.

teach.b: The title was Sultan-ul-Qaum. Sultan is a king, and qaum is a people, a community, a nation: the king of the community. None of it, tradition says, starts with a crown.

teach.h: RAISED BY MATA SUNDARI, SINGING KIRTAN.
teach.b: In Mata Sundari's house, tradition says, he learned kirtan, singing the Guru's hymns, and kept singing them all his life.

Then he was handed on to Nawab Kapur Singh, who led the Sikh bands. Under him, tradition says, the boy worked: looking after horses, serving in the langar, the free kitchen, doing the jobs nobody writes poems about.
Kapur Singh watched him, and in time named him to carry the leadership on.

So by the time the gathering at Amritsar chose him to head the Dal Khalsa, he had been formed by two people who led by serving: a widow who kept the community together with letters, and a nawab who fanned the congregation.
That's the leadership Sikhs prize in him. The Sikh scripture is wary of rulers who think power makes them great.

Guru Nanak, in a hard line here in paraphrase, compares the kings of his day to tigers and their officials to dogs. Jassa Singh's story is told as the other kind. And the title is about the qaum, the people, not the land.
A sultan of a country owns ground; a leader of the qaum carries people. Sikhs remember him as a fighter who stood at the front, and as a man who, tradition says, was still singing the morning hymns.

how: Sikhs remember Jassa Singh Ahluwalia as Sultan-ul-Qaum, and his story is told in gurdwara talks and Sikh history lessons as an example of a leader formed by kirtan and seva.

o: a Mughal governor who ruled Lahore in the hard years
the poet who wrote down the story of the Sikh bands
a leader raised on kirtan who went on to head the Dal Khalsa

he became leader without ever doing humble work

games.q: you're a young Sikh in Nawab Kapur Singh's camp. you've been raised in the Guru's household and you sing beautifully. you're handed the horses to look after. what do you do?
o: ask for a job more fitting for someone like you.
do it, and do it well.
do it badly so they'll give you something better.
games.why: tradition says he served at the plain jobs, and that Kapur Singh, watching, chose him to carry the leadership on.

practice: Think of somewhere you have a little say, a family dinner, a project, a shift at work, and find the job nobody wants there: the horse nobody grooms, the dish nobody washes.
See yourself doing it quietly, before anyone asks, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Jassa Singh. Raised, tradition says, in Mata Sundari's household and trained by Nawab Kapur Singh, he led the Dal Khalsa and was honored as Sultan-ul-Qaum, king of the community. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi spelling of the Persian title Sultan-ul-Qaum, king of the community, given to Jassa Singh Ahluwalia.

carryVoice: Your line: leader of the qaum. He started with the horses and the hymns. Eight hundred sixty days now.
